readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 16:1-17:58. God chooses David, and David defeats Goliath. Read slowly, and notice what each side says about who will win and why.
settingTheScene: After Saul’s rejection, God sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint one of Jesse’s sons as king. The chosen one is the youngest, a shepherd. David enters Saul’s service as a musician, and then, in the valley of Elah, faces the Philistine champion Goliath when the whole army of Israel is paralyzed with fear. These chapters introduce the central human figure of the Old Testament narrative.
observation: God tells Samuel, “Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons” (16:1).
“Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (16:7).
David is brought in from the sheep, “ruddy, with beautiful eyes and handsome”, and the LORD says, “Arise, anoint him, for this is he” (16:12).
“The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward” (16:13), while the Spirit departs from Saul (16:14).
Goliath, who stood about nine feet tall, taunts Israel for forty days (17:4, 16).
David says, “Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” (17:26).
David refuses Saul’s armor and takes five smooth stones and his sling (17:38-40).
“You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts… that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel” (17:45-46).
interpretation:
The story of David’s anointing begins with a reversal of expectations. Samuel looks at Eliab, the tall oldest son, and thinks, “Surely the LORD’s anointed is before him.” But the LORD says, “Do not look on his appearance… For the LORD sees not as man sees.” This echoes the story of Saul, who looked the part and failed. God chooses the youngest, the one who was left with the sheep. It is a repeated pattern in the Bible: Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph, Moses, and now David.

The Spirit’s movement is dramatic. He rushes on David and leaves Saul. Saul is now troubled by a harmful spirit, and David’s music soothes him. The king who has been rejected receives comfort from the one who will replace him.

The Goliath narrative is often read as a lesson in courage, but its real theme is who fights for Israel. The whole army, Saul included, sees Goliath’s size and trembles. David sees Goliath’s defiance of God. For David the question is not whether Goliath is big, but whether the living God is big enough. He has fought lions and bears, and he credits the LORD with those victories.

David’s declaration before the battle is the heart of the chapter. “The battle is the LORD’s.” He does not rely on Saul’s armor or on conventional weapons. He wants the world to know that God can save without sword or spear. The victory is not just David’s. It is for all Israel, a public sign that there is a God in Israel.

There is a deeper pattern. David stands alone as a representative for the people. If he wins, they win. If he loses, they are slaves. The people share in the victory of their champion without lifting a sword.
connection: Jesus is the greater David: born in Bethlehem, a shepherd, and the anointed King (Micah 5:2; John 10:11). He is the champion who fights in our place, defeating sin, death, and the devil (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14-15). The victory is ours without our having lifted a sword. Paul says, “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).
application:
Ask what your “Goliath” is, the thing that has been mocking you for forty days.

Remember that Christ has already fought and won. Stand in his victory.

Ask the Lord to teach you to see people as he sees them, by the heart.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you to see as he sees, and to trust him in the battle you face.
Thank Jesus, your champion, who defeated sin and death.
Name a giant in your life and give it to him.
